claim: The IR-DR assay identified more than 130 positively acting compounds that are chemically diverse.
source: The assay identified a chemically diverse set of >130 positively acting compounds, highly enriched in true positives, that targeted 73 proteins regulating IR pathways.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the results.

claim: The positively acting compounds identified by the IR-DR assay are highly enriched in true positives.
source: The assay identified a chemically diverse set of >130 positively acting compounds, highly enriched in true positives, that targeted 73 proteins regulating IR pathways.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and validated through multiple approaches described in the manuscript.

source: The assay identified a chemically diverse set of >130 positively acting compounds, highly enriched in true positives, that targeted 73 proteins regulating IR pathways.

claim: The multi-gene RNA assay score reflected the quantitative pharmacological properties of epidermal growth factor receptor-related tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
source: Our multi-gene RNA assay score reflected the quantitative pharmacological properties of a set of epidermal growth factor receptor-related tyrosine kinase inhibitors, providing insight into drug target specificity; an observation supported by deep learning-based genome-wide predicted pharmacology.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated with data in Figure 3.

claim: The relationship between in vitro drug potency and IR-DR assay score was supported by deep learning-based genome-wide predicted pharmacology.
source: Our multi-gene RNA assay score reflected the quantitative pharmacological properties of a set of epidermal growth factor receptor-related tyrosine kinase inhibitors, providing insight into drug target specificity; an observation supported by deep learning-based genome-wide predicted pharmacology.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section using DeepPurpose modeling.

claim: Several drugs identified are suitable for evaluation in patients with acute or severe chronic IR.
source: Several drugs identified are suitable for evaluation in patients, particularly those with either acute or severe chronic IR.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the findings of the study.

claim: Systemic insulin resistance (IR) is a multi-organ pathophysiological state.
source: Systemic insulin resistance (IR) is a multi-organ pathophysiological state and an early characteristic of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Systemic insulin resistance (IR) is an early characteristic of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
source: Systemic insulin resistance (IR) is a multi-organ pathophysiological state and an early characteristic of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: IR contributes to the pathobiology of neurodegeneration.
source: IR contributes to the pathobiology of neurodegeneration (Norambuena et al., 2017), heart failure (Wamil et al., 2021) and viral infections, such as COVID-19 (Ceriello et al., 2020; Donath, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: IR contributes to the pathobiology of heart failure.
source: IR contributes to the pathobiology of neurodegeneration (Norambuena et al., 2017), heart failure (Wamil et al., 2021) and viral infections, such as COVID-19 (Ceriello et al., 2020; Donath, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: IR contributes to the pathobiology of viral infections, such as COVID-19.
source: IR contributes to the pathobiology of neurodegeneration (Norambuena et al., 2017), heart failure (Wamil et al., 2021) and viral infections, such as COVID-19 (Ceriello et al., 2020; Donath, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Several T2DM drug treatments indirectly reduce IR following improved metabolic homeostasis.
source: Several T2DM drug treatments indirectly reduce IR following improved metabolic homeostasis, making them candidate treatments for various diseases (Donath, 2021; Everett et al., 2018; Norambuena et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: T2DM drug treatments that reduce IR are candidate treatments for various diseases.
source: Several T2DM drug treatments indirectly reduce IR following improved metabolic homeostasis, making them candidate treatments for various diseases (Donath, 2021; Everett et al., 2018; Norambuena et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Drug repurposing (DR) aims to accelerate the discovery and reduce the costs of new treatments.
source: Drug repurposing (DR) aims to accelerate the discovery and reduce the costs of new treatments.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle of drug repurposing in the introduction.

claim: Drug transcriptome responses in cells represent one of the most extensive resources for drug repurposing.
source: Drug transcriptome responses in cells represent one of the most extensive resources (Subramanian et al., 2017), while transcriptomics is also an ideal technology to capture complex biological processes in human tissues (Jenkinson et al., 2016; Timmons et al., 2018; Timmons et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Transcriptomics is an ideal technology to capture complex biological processes in human tissues.
source: Drug transcriptome responses in cells represent one of the most extensive resources (Subramanian et al., 2017), while transcriptomics is also an ideal technology to capture complex biological processes in human tissues (Jenkinson et al., 2016; Timmons et al., 2018; Timmons et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Effectiveness at reversing molecular responses to disease helps to predict drug efficacy in cancer.
source: Effectiveness at reversing of the molecular responses to disease (Wagner et al., 2015) helps to predict drug efficacy in cancer (Brown and Patel, 2018; Iorio et al., 2018; Karatzas et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Successful application of DR specifically to oncology may reflect that drug profiles are typically generated in tumour cell lines.
source: Successful application of DR specifically to oncology may reflect that drug profiles are typically generated in tumour cell lines (Subramanian et al., 2017) and that barriers to clinical validation can be lower compared with many other diseases.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Barriers to clinical validation in oncology can be lower compared with many other diseases.
source: Successful application of DR specifically to oncology may reflect that drug profiles are typically generated in tumour cell lines (Subramanian et al., 2017) and that barriers to clinical validation can be lower compared with many other diseases.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the introduction.

claim: Identifying informative disease signatures for DR in cells is challenging.
source: Identifying informative disease signatures for DR in cells is challenging (Chen et al., 2020; Karatzas et al., 2017; Regan-Fendt et al., 2019), particularly when no positive controls exist (Williams et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: There are currently no reliable human cellular models for systemic IR.
source: Currently, there are no reliable human cellular models for systemic IR, while it remains unclear if multi-gene assays can capture quantitative pharmacological relationships suitable for optimising drug design.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation in the introduction.

claim: It remains unclear if multi-gene assays can capture quantitative pharmacological relationships suitable for optimising drug design.
source: Currently, there are no reliable human cellular models for systemic IR, while it remains unclear if multi-gene assays can capture quantitative pharmacological relationships suitable for optimising drug design.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Clinically effective drugs typically target several proteins, many of which are unknown.
source: However, clinically effective drugs typically target several proteins, many of which are unknown (Keenan et al., 2018), highlighting the limitations of single-target drug development programmes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: The study utilized more than 2000 tissue profiles generated in the authors' laboratories and one other laboratory.
source: For IR we also have effective non-drug treatments (Nakhuda et al., 2016; Slentz et al., 2016; Timmons et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2017), and this enabled production of a novel human-based IR-DR assay – using more than 2000 tissue profiles generated in our laboratories (Nakhuda et al., 2016; Slentz et al., 2016; Timmons et al., 2018) and one other (Civelek et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study with citations.

claim: Performance of the RNA-based multi-gene assays was judged against positive control in vivo drug signatures.
source: Performance of the present RNA-based multi-gene assays was judged against positive control in vivo drug signatures (Stathias et al., 2020), genome-wide association (Lotta et al., 2017; Vujkovic et al., 2020) and blood proteome-based assays (Gudmundsdottir et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the validation methodology used in the study with citations.

claim: Performance of the RNA-based multi-gene assays was judged against genome-wide association studies.
source: Performance of the present RNA-based multi-gene assays was judged against positive control in vivo drug signatures (Stathias et al., 2020), genome-wide association (Lotta et al., 2017; Vujkovic et al., 2020) and blood proteome-based assays (Gudmundsdottir et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the validation methodology used in the study with citations.

claim: Performance of the RNA-based multi-gene assays was judged against blood proteome-based assays.
source: Performance of the present RNA-based multi-gene assays was judged against positive control in vivo drug signatures (Stathias et al., 2020), genome-wide association (Lotta et al., 2017; Vujkovic et al., 2020) and blood proteome-based assays (Gudmundsdottir et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the validation methodology used in the study with citations.

claim: Validation of the in vitro results for more than 2500 drugs relied on DL-based modelling of drug-to-protein interactions.
source: Validation of the in vitro results for >2500 drugs (Subramanian et al., 2017) relied on a variety of protein, drug- and disease-centric (Parisi et al., 2020) criteria: DL-based modelling of drug-to-protein interactions; targeted gene knock down; and published evidence that the drug reduced IR in vivo (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the validation methodology used in the study.

claim: Validation of the in vitro results for more than 2500 drugs relied on targeted gene knock down.
source: Validation of the in vitro results for >2500 drugs (Subramanian et al., 2017) relied on a variety of protein, drug- and disease-centric (Parisi et al., 2020) criteria: DL-based modelling of drug-to-protein interactions; targeted gene knock down; and published evidence that the drug reduced IR in vivo (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the validation methodology used in the study.

claim: Validation of the in vitro results for more than 2500 drugs relied on published evidence that the drug reduced IR in vivo.
source: Validation of the in vitro results for >2500 drugs (Subramanian et al., 2017) relied on a variety of protein, drug- and disease-centric (Parisi et al., 2020) criteria: DL-based modelling of drug-to-protein interactions; targeted gene knock down; and published evidence that the drug reduced IR in vivo (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the validation methodology used in the study.

claim: HOMA2-IR was used to quantify IR.
source: Homeostasis model assessment version 2 (HOMA2-IR) was used to quantify IR (Wallace et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study with citation.

claim: RNA biomarkers consistently related to fasting IR across tissues were combined with those regulated in common across tissues following lifestyle-based reversal of IR.
source: RNA biomarkers consistently related to fasting IR ('disease') across tissues were combined with those regulated in common across tissues following lifestyle-based reversal of IR ('treatment').
evidence: This describes the methodology used to develop the IR-DR signature.

claim: Biomarkers were ranked based on consistent direction and strength of association across human adipose and muscle.
source: Biomarkers were ranked based on consistent direction and strength of association across two major human organs targeted by insulin (human adipose and muscle) because most orally dosed drugs will act systemically.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to develop the IR-DR signature.

claim: Most orally dosed drugs will act systemically.
source: Biomarkers were ranked based on consistent direction and strength of association across two major human organs targeted by insulin (human adipose and muscle) because most orally dosed drugs will act systemically.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the methodology.

claim: The study considered the performance of only four RNA-based IR-DR assays.
source: In the present study, we considered the performance of only four RNA-based IR-DR assays (Appendix 1—figure 1; Ganter et al., 2006); testing their ability to match the in vivo directionality of positive controls, thiazolidinedione (TZD) and oestrogen, expression signatures correctly (Hevener et al., 2018; Sears et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The top-scoring RNA signature (Signature 3A) was a statistically ranked combination of disease- and treatment-associated genes (n = 120 genes).
source: The top-scoring RNA signature (Signature 3A from Appendix 1—figure 1) was a statistically ranked combination of disease- and treatment-associated genes (n = 120 genes) outranked selection by hub connectedness, recapitulated cellular gene expression patterns indicative of TZD treatment responses in vivo in muscle (moderated Z-score, p<0.0000008, Appendix 1—figure 2) and is referred to as the IR-DR signature/assay hereafter (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This describes the primary finding of the feature selection process with statistical support.

claim: Signature 3A outranked selection by hub connectedness.
source: The top-scoring RNA signature (Signature 3A from Appendix 1—figure 1) was a statistically ranked combination of disease- and treatment-associated genes (n = 120 genes) outranked selection by hub connectedness, recapitulated cellular gene expression patterns indicative of TZD treatment responses in vivo in muscle (moderated Z-score, p<0.0000008, Appendix 1—figure 2) and is referred to as the IR-DR signature/assay hereafter (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This describes the primary finding of the feature selection process.

claim: Signature 3A recapitulated cellular gene expression patterns indicative of TZD treatment responses in vivo in muscle (moderated Z-score, p<0.0000008).
source: The top-scoring RNA signature (Signature 3A from Appendix 1—figure 1) was a statistically ranked combination of disease- and treatment-associated genes (n = 120 genes) outranked selection by hub connectedness, recapitulated cellular gene expression patterns indicative of TZD treatment responses in vivo in muscle (moderated Z-score, p<0.0000008, Appendix 1—figure 2) and is referred to as the IR-DR signature/assay hereafter (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This describes the validation of Signature 3A with statistical support.

claim: Lack of superiority for the assay designed using hub connectedness may reflect that inclusion of multi-tissue treatment response biomarkers supersedes any benefit of using network weighting.
source: Lack of superiority for the assay designed using hub connectedness may be considered at odds with other studies (Cheng et al., 2012) but could reflect that inclusion of multi-tissue treatment response biomarkers supersedes any benefit of using network weighting.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results with citation.

claim: Several Genome-wide Association Study (GWAS) IR and T2DM-derived signatures were unable to match positive control drugs in vivo.
source: Several Genome-wide Association Study (GWAS) IR and T2DM (Lotta et al., 2017; Vujkovic et al., 2020)-derived signatures (e.g. Signature 4, Appendix 1—figure 1) were considered but were unable to match positive control drugs in vivo.
evidence: This describes a negative result from the validation process with citations.

claim: The T2DM blood proteome signature had a weak association with one positive control drug.
source: The T2DM blood proteome signature (Gudmundsdottir et al., 2020) had a weak association with one positive control drug.
evidence: This describes a result from the validation process with citation.

claim: The study utilized aggregated scores from across nine human cell lines to identify cell-type agnostic drug responses.
source: To achieve this, we utilised aggregated scores (the maximum quantile statistic from the within-cell line-normalised scores) from across nine human cell lines.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Aggregating scores across cell types increases the sample size per drug by at least ninefold.
source: This approach also increases the sample size per drug by at least ninefold, making any inferences more reliable (Subramanian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the methodology with citation.

claim: Members of each drug 'class' were segregated with either active or neutral IR-DR scores.
source: Critically, we noted that members of each drug 'class' (drugs sharing a nominal primary protein target in common) were segregated with either active or neutral IR-DR scores, with extremely few drug classes having both positive- and negative-scoring compounds.
evidence: This describes a finding from the analysis of drug classes.

claim: Only 10% of the database matched the IR-DR signature (n = 254).
source: Only 10% of the database matched the IR-DR signature (n = 254, Appendix 1—figure 3 and Table S3), and 138 compounds (after excluding assay codes with ambiguous compound labels) positively regulated the IR-DR signature (potential treatments), 45% of which were kinase inhibitors (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This describes a primary finding from the drug screening with specific numbers.

claim: 138 compounds positively regulated the IR-DR signature.
source: Only 10% of the database matched the IR-DR signature (n = 254, Appendix 1—figure 3 and Table S3), and 138 compounds (after excluding assay codes with ambiguous compound labels) positively regulated the IR-DR signature (potential treatments), 45% of which were kinase inhibitors (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This describes a primary finding from the drug screening with specific numbers.

claim: 45% of the positively acting compounds were kinase inhibitors.
source: Only 10% of the database matched the IR-DR signature (n = 254, Appendix 1—figure 3 and Table S3), and 138 compounds (after excluding assay codes with ambiguous compound labels) positively regulated the IR-DR signature (potential treatments), 45% of which were kinase inhibitors (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This describes a primary finding from the drug screening with specific percentages.

claim: Most negative acting drugs targeted tubulin and cell cycle proteins or were pro-inflammatory agents.
source: Most negative acting drugs targeted tubulin and cell cycle proteins or were pro-inflammatory agents (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This describes a finding from the analysis of negative acting drugs.

claim: Positive and negative acting compounds did not differ in average physiochemical properties.
source: Positive and negative acting compounds did not differ in average physiochemical properties (Appendix 1—figure 6), while assays based on GWAS-selected genes for IR (Lotta et al., 2017; Vujkovic et al., 2020) and T2DM produced no discernible pattern of in vitro hits.
evidence: This describes a finding from the analysis of compound properties with citations.

claim: Assays based on GWAS-selected genes for IR and T2DM produced no discernible pattern of in vitro hits.
source: Positive and negative acting compounds did not differ in average physiochemical properties (Appendix 1—figure 6), while assays based on GWAS-selected genes for IR (Lotta et al., 2017; Vujkovic et al., 2020) and T2DM produced no discernible pattern of in vitro hits.
evidence: This describes a negative result from the validation process with citations.

claim: The pharmacology of the 138 positive compounds indicated that a substantial number of targeted aspects of insulin signalling were known, empirically, to reverse IR in vivo.
source: The pharmacology of the 138 positive compounds indicated that a substantial number of targeted aspects of insulin signalling were known, empirically, to reverse IR in vivo (Table 1).
evidence: This describes a finding from the analysis of positive compounds with reference to a table.

claim: Inhibition of glucosylceramide synthase reverses IR and fatty liver disease.
source: Compounds identified varied in nature from inhibitors of glucosylceramide synthase, which reverses IR and fatty liver disease (Aerts et al., 2007; Herrera Moro Chao et al., 2019), to 10 mTOR inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: The study identified 10 mTOR inhibitors as positively acting compounds.
source: Compounds identified varied in nature from inhibitors of glucosylceramide synthase, which reverses IR and fatty liver disease (Aerts et al., 2007; Herrera Moro Chao et al., 2019), to 10 mTOR inhibitors.
evidence: This describes a finding from the drug screening.

claim: The mTOR complex, mTORC1, coordinates a negative feedback loop on insulin signalling through activation of GRB10 or via S6K1.
source: The mTOR complex, mTORC1, coordinates a negative feedback loop on insulin signalling, for example, through activation of GRB10 or via S6K1 (Um et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claim: mTORC1 signalling is regulated by protein kinase C (PKC).
source: mTORC1 signalling is also regulated by protein kinase C (PKC) (Zhan et al., 2019), and specific PKC isoforms are dysregulated in ageing, metabolic, neurodegenerative and inflammatory diseases (Li et al., 2015; Sajan et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claim: Specific PKC isoforms are dysregulated in ageing, metabolic, neurodegenerative and inflammatory diseases.
source: mTORC1 signalling is also regulated by protein kinase C (PKC) (Zhan et al., 2019), and specific PKC isoforms are dysregulated in ageing, metabolic, neurodegenerative and inflammatory diseases (Li et al., 2015; Sajan et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: The broad-spectrum PKC inhibitor, bisindolylmaleimide I, induced a strong positive IR signature score (+87).
source: We observed that the broad-spectrum PKC inhibitor, bisindolylmaleimide I, induced a strong positive IR signature score (+87) and the related compound, ruboxistaurin, reverses IR in vivo (Guo et al., 2020; Naruse et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes a finding from the drug screening with specific score.

claim: Ruboxistaurin reverses IR in vivo.
source: We observed that the broad-spectrum PKC inhibitor, bisindolylmaleimide I, induced a strong positive IR signature score (+87) and the related compound, ruboxistaurin, reverses IR in vivo (Guo et al., 2020; Naruse et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: Bisindolylmaleimide IX was inactive in the IR-DR assay.
source: In contrast, bisindolylmaleimide IX, a 20-fold more potent broad-spectrum PKC inhibitor, was inactive in the IR-DR assay, probably reflecting its greater non-specific pharmacology (against other kinase families).
evidence: This describes a finding from the drug screening.

claim: Bisindolylmaleimide IX's inactivity in the IR-DR assay probably reflects its greater non-specific pharmacology against other kinase families.
source: In contrast, bisindolylmaleimide IX, a 20-fold more potent broad-spectrum PKC inhibitor, was inactive in the IR-DR assay, probably reflecting its greater non-specific pharmacology (against other kinase families).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the finding.

claim: Three PKC activators induced negative IR-DR scores: phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate = –87, ingenol = –96 and prostratin = –97.
source: Three so-called PKC activators (French et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020) induced negative IR-DR scores (phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate = –87, ingenol = –96 and prostratin = –97).
evidence: This describes a finding from the drug screening with specific scores and citations.

claim: Knock-down of PKC-beta yielded a positive IR-DR score (+74).
source: While >95% of all RNAi assays produced no significant scores, knock-down (KD) of PKC-beta (+74) and PKC-theta (+97) yielded positive IR-DR scores, while loss of PKC-alpha (–75) and -eta (–75) produced negative IR-DR scores and overexpression (OE) of PKC-alpha was positive scoring (+85).
evidence: This describes a finding from the RNAi validation with specific score.

claim: Knock-down of PKC-theta yielded a positive IR-DR score (+97).
source: While >95% of all RNAi assays produced no significant scores, knock-down (KD) of PKC-beta (+74) and PKC-theta (+97) yielded positive IR-DR scores, while loss of PKC-alpha (–75) and -eta (–75) produced negative IR-DR scores and overexpression (OE) of PKC-alpha was positive scoring (+85).
evidence: This describes a finding from the RNAi validation with specific score.

claim: Loss of PKC-alpha produced a negative IR-DR score (–75).
source: While >95% of all RNAi assays produced no significant scores, knock-down (KD) of PKC-beta (+74) and PKC-theta (+97) yielded positive IR-DR scores, while loss of PKC-alpha (–75) and -eta (–75) produced negative IR-DR scores and overexpression (OE) of PKC-alpha was positive scoring (+85).
evidence: This describes a finding from the RNAi validation with specific score.

claim: Loss of PKC-eta produced a negative IR-DR score (–75).
source: While >95% of all RNAi assays produced no significant scores, knock-down (KD) of PKC-beta (+74) and PKC-theta (+97) yielded positive IR-DR scores, while loss of PKC-alpha (–75) and -eta (–75) produced negative IR-DR scores and overexpression (OE) of PKC-alpha was positive scoring (+85).
evidence: This describes a finding from the RNAi validation with specific score.

claim: Overexpression of PKC-alpha was positive scoring (+85).
source: While >95% of all RNAi assays produced no significant scores, knock-down (KD) of PKC-beta (+74) and PKC-theta (+97) yielded positive IR-DR scores, while loss of PKC-alpha (–75) and -eta (–75) produced negative IR-DR scores and overexpression (OE) of PKC-alpha was positive scoring (+85).
evidence: This describes a finding from the RNAi validation with specific score.

claim: The multi-gene IR-DR assay identifies numerous true-positive drugs.
source: The multi-gene IR-DR assay therefore identifies numerous true-positive drugs (Table 1) and reflects isoform-specific activity, strongly validating the cell-agnostic aggregation methodology.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results with reference to a table.

claim: The multi-gene IR-DR assay reflects isoform-specific activity.
source: The multi-gene IR-DR assay therefore identifies numerous true-positive drugs (Table 1) and reflects isoform-specific activity, strongly validating the cell-agnostic aggregation methodology.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results.

claim: The 138 positive scoring IR-DR drugs target 1007 proteins.
source: The 138 positive scoring IR-DR drugs target 1007 proteins (Mendez et al., 2019; Moret et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a finding from the analysis of drug targets with citations.

claim: Of the 1007 proteins targeted by positive scoring drugs, 465 genes had single-gene KD or OE scores.
source: Of these, 465 genes had single-gene KD or OE scores, aggregated across 6–9 cell lines (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This describes a finding from the analysis of drug targets.

claim: Seventy-three targets (15.7%) yielded a significant IR-DR score.
source: Seventy-three targets (15.7%) yielded a significant IR-DR score; double the assay hit rate (p<0.0001, see Methods and Figure 2).
evidence: This describes a finding from the RNAi validation with statistical support.

claim: The 73 validated targets represent double the assay hit rate (p<0.0001).
source: Seventy-three targets (15.7%) yielded a significant IR-DR score; double the assay hit rate (p<0.0001, see Methods and Figure 2).
evidence: This describes a finding from the RNAi validation with statistical support.

claim: The 73 validated targets regulated 'peptidyl-serine phosphorylation-related processes' (q-value <1 × 10–23).
source: Predictably, due to input bias (Timmons et al., 2015), these targets regulated 'peptidyl-serine phosphorylation-related processes' (q-value <1 × 10–23).
evidence: This describes a finding from the pathway analysis with statistical support and citation.

claim: None of the 73 validated targets belonged to the IR-DR gene signature.
source: None belonged to the IR-DR gene signature (Appendix 1—figure 8), but they did belong to numerous common pathways (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This describes a finding from the analysis of validated targets.

claim: The 73 validated targets belonged to numerous common pathways with the IR-DR signature.
source: None belonged to the IR-DR gene signature (Appendix 1—figure 8), but they did belong to numerous common pathways (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This describes a finding from the pathway analysis.

claim: An effective DR signature captures the pathway biology of the disease and/or treatment but does not necessarily include the nominal drug targets.
source: These observations are consistent with the idea that an effective DR signature captures the pathway biology of the disease and/or treatment (Brown and Patel, 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Karatzas et al., 2017; Keenan et al., 2018; Regan-Fendt et al., 2019; Wagner et al., 2015; Woo et al., 2015) but does not necessarily include the nominal drug targets (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings with multiple citations.

claim: The relationship between in vitro drug potency and IR-DR assay score for 37 compounds nominally targeting EGFR tyrosine kinase was investigated.
source: The relationship between in vitro drug potency and IR-DR assay score for 37 compounds (Appendix 1—figure 5), nominally targeting epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR or HER1) tyrosine kinase, was investigated.
evidence: This describes the methodology for investigating quantitative pharmacology.

claim: EGFR is a stress-induced inflammatory protein that has recently emerged as a target for treating metabolic disease and neurodegeneration.
source: This stress-induced inflammatory protein has recently emerged as a target for treating metabolic disease and neurodegeneration (Donath, 2021; Menden et al., 2019; Norambuena et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: Amphiregulin, an endogenous EGFR ligand, is induced by high-fat feeding to drive TNF-mediated IR.
source: One endogenous EGFR ligand, amphiregulin, is induced by high-fat feeding to drive TNF-mediated IR (Skurski et al., 2020), while EGFR is overexpressed in astrocytes of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claim: EGFR is overexpressed in astrocytes of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: One endogenous EGFR ligand, amphiregulin, is induced by high-fat feeding to drive TNF-mediated IR (Skurski et al., 2020), while EGFR is overexpressed in astrocytes of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: The EGFR inhibitor afatinib (IR-DR score = 77) attenuates astrocyte activation.
source: The EGFR inhibitor afatinib (IR-DR score = 77) attenuates astrocyte activation (Chen et al., 2019) while inhibition of EGFR can reduce FOXK1 and FOXK2 phosphorylation (Klaeger et al., 2017) to normalise mTORC1-regulated autophagy and reduce IR (Bowman et al., 2014; Jahng et al., 2019).
